lines.text: A further indication of this is the present popularity of the
stories of Adalbert Stifter with their descriptions of nature
and of a type of life that fulfils its destiny in the midst of
nature. And is not nature becoming increasingly absorbed in
city culture and the technological organization of human
life? Is it not being increasingly despoiled of its original peace
and tranquillity and the mysterious sway of its inherent
vitalities disturbed? It was still possible for Schiller to write:
"There is perfection in the world of nature wherever man
with his torment does not intrude." But where is it that man
does not nowadays intrude? What does he not disturb with
his tormenting unrest? What sphere is still left within the
framework of our civilization, one might almost say on the
whole earth, where in truth the peace and stillness and
purity of nature reign undisturbed? The noise of modern
traffic and the wail of modern jazz destroy the peace of even
the remotest spots. Modern motor roads and the building
of huge industrial plants utterly efface the natural beauties
of our landscape.
It may perhaps be retorted that this is a romantic,
aesthetic point of view. Is not this development inevitable?
Is it not a question of harsh necessities which are rooted in
the evolution of modern life? No doubt we are faced here to
a large extent by sheer necessity. But should that blind us to
the fact that nature which is thus integrated with the
historical development and fate of man is being disfigured
and defaced in the process? And does it all rest on sheer
necessity? Where does a reasonable requirement begin and
where does it end? Is not the ancient myth justified which
suggests that the curse resting on nature has its origin in the
sin of man? How much of this destructive process is the
consequence not of the real exigencies of life, but of the
demand for elaborate forms of pleasure, and the divorce of
human life from nature? How much flows from the sheer
desperate striving after profits—a mentality which has lost
all respect for nature and ruthlessly exploits it, which regards
every forest from the point of view of the productive timber
it contains, every stream as a source of power to be canalized
